title: Priests and Kings
objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt split between priests and kings.
summary: After the New Kingdom, the high priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes while kings ruled the north from Tanis. The priests also rescued robbed royal mummies.

cards.headline: After about 1069 BCE, kings ruled Egypt’s north and priests ran the south.
cards.body: The New Kingdom was over. Egypt didn’t fall; it split. And the most powerful man in the south wore a priest’s robes.

cards.headline: A priest takes the title
cards.body: Herihor was high priest of the god Amun at Karnak, in Thebes. Late in the 20th dynasty, as Egypt became disunited, he took the full title of a pharaoh and founded a line of priest-kings who ruled the south. Picture your local archbishop quietly adding “King” to his business card.

cards.headline: Two capitals
cards.body: In the 21st Dynasty the split settled in. Kings ruled Lower Egypt from Tanis, in the Delta, while the High Priests of Amun at Thebes grew more and more powerful. Remember Level 1’s valleys between the peaks? This is the third: the Third Intermediate Period, when the land was divided again. Later a Libyan leader, Shoshenq, founded a new dynasty at Tanis. The one who finally took all of Egypt would come from Kush, in the south.
cards.callout: North: kings at Tanis. South: priests at Thebes.

cards.headline: Rescuing the dead kings
cards.body: Meanwhile, the royal tombs at Thebes were being robbed. Priests and officials of the 21st Dynasty gathered damaged royal mummies, rewrapped them and hid several New Kingdom kings together in a secret cache at Deir el-Bahari. It worked: nobody found it until 1881. Among the kings inside was Ramesses II. Ramesses the Great, sharing a hiding place, saved by priests.

A time when the land was divided, often under local rulers
A time when the Nile failed to flood
